key_insight: Genotyping malaria infections throughout follow-up provided a more comprehensive assessment of CIS43LS efficacy than time-to-first-infection analysis, with no evidence of escape-associated changes in its target epitope.
clinical_relevance: For malaria prevention research—not AI cancer drug discovery—genotypic endpoints can clarify protection against repeated infections and differences by baseline infection status.
method: Genotyped all detected Plasmodium falciparum infections in a phase 2 trial involving 330 Malian adults.
Estimated molecular force of infection: the rate of newly acquired parasite strains.
Compared strain-acquisition rates between CIS43LS and placebo arms over six months.
evidence_signal: Six-month efficacy against new-strain acquisition was 86.5% (95% CI: 80.1–90.8) at 40 mg/kg and 70.7% (61.0–78.0) at 10 mg/kg, with greater precision than time-to-first analysis in monthly and baseline-status comparisons.
watch_item: The absence of detected escape polymorphisms over six months in this adult cohort does not rule out escape in other populations or with longer follow-up.
paper_title: Genotypic infection endpoint analysis to understand efficacy and escape potential of the malaria monoclonal antibody CIS43LS
